p: For the maximum, a larger digit in a higher place gives more, so the leftmost digit that isn't already 9 should become 9 (all its copies too, as required). For the minimum, the most significant place is worth the most, so replacing the first digit by 0 reduces the number as much as possible. Digits are chosen independently for the max and the min.

2566.takeaway: Maximise by turning the first non-9 digit into 9 everywhere; minimise by turning the first digit into 0 everywhere.

blocks.h: Why prefix sums and binary search?
p: For each query the cost is a sum of |x − q|. Elements below q need q − x each, elements at or above need x − q. Sorting makes these two groups a prefix and a suffix; prefix sums give each group's total in O(1) and `bisect_left` finds the split in O(log n), so each query costs O(log n) instead of O(n).

2602.takeaway: Sort + prefix sums + bisect: split the array at q and compute the raise and lower costs from prefix sums.

blocks.h: Why does greedy by difference work?
p: Giving piece i to mouse 1 changes the total by exactly `reward1[i] − reward2[i]` relative to the baseline. Exactly k pieces must switch, and the total is the baseline plus the sum of the chosen gains, so choosing the k largest gains is optimal (even negative gains are taken when fewer than k positive ones exist).

2611.takeaway: Start from everything going to mouse 2 and switch the k pieces with the largest reward1 − reward2.

Suffix OR: all numbers to the right
OR of numbers to the left

blocks.h: Why put all doublings on one number?
p: Shifting an element left by t moves its highest bit up t places, and the highest bit dominates the OR. Splitting the shifts across two numbers gives a smaller top bit than shifting one number by the total. So the best plan multiplies a single element by 2^k, and prefix/suffix ORs let us test each candidate in O(1).

2680.takeaway: All k doublings go to a single number (it pushes the highest bit furthest); prefix and suffix ORs evaluate each choice in O(1).

blocks.h: Why `tight` and why prune on `s > max_sum`?
p: Counting numbers up to a bound digit by digit needs to remember whether we are still equal to the bound's prefix: only then is the next digit limited. Once a smaller digit appears, everything after is unconstrained. The check `s > max_sum` stops branches whose digit sum has already exceeded the limit. The state space is (positions × sums × 2), small compared with the 10²² numbers in range.

2719.takeaway: Digit DP with a tight flag and running digit sum: count up to num2, subtract up to num1, add back num1 if it qualifies.

p: The earliest position where the string can be made smaller dominates lexicographic order, and decrementing a longer run only improves later positions, but the run must stop before an 'a' (turning it into 'z' would make it worse). So take the first maximal run of non-'a' letters after any leading 'a's.

2734.takeaway: Skip leading 'a's, then decrement the first maximal run of non-'a' letters; an all-'a' string changes its last letter to 'z'.

p: parent `[-1,0,0,1,1,2]`, letters `'acaabc'` → 8 (masks use bits a=0, b=1, c=2):

The multiset of letters on the path between u and v equals the root-to-u letters plus the root-to-v letters, minus twice the root-to-lca letters. Parities are mod 2, so the doubled part vanishes and the parity mask of the path is `mask[u] ^ mask[v]`. A palindrome arrangement exists iff that mask has at most one set bit, i.e. is 0 or a power of two.

2791.takeaway: Letter-parity masks from the root: the path parity is mask[u] ^ mask[v]; count pairs whose XOR has at most one set bit.

blocks.h: Why a max-heap rather than BFS?
p: We maximise the minimum along the path. Always expanding the cell with the highest current path safeness (like Dijkstra with `min` in place of `+`) guarantees that the first time a cell is popped, its value is the best possible for it. The target's value on the first pop is the answer.

2812.takeaway: BFS for thief distances, then a best-first search (max-heap) where a path's value is the minimum distance on it.

blocks.h: Why count r − l at once?
p: The array is sorted. If `nums[l] + nums[r] < target`, then replacing `nums[r]` by any smaller element between l and r keeps the sum below target, so all r − l partners of `nums[l]` work. Then `l` advances. If the sum is too large, `nums[r]` is too big for every remaining `l`, so `r` decreases.

2824.takeaway: Sorted two pointers: when nums[l] + nums[r] < target, all r − l partners of nums[l] qualify.

p: Moves commute: only the totals matter, not the order. The farthest end point sends every '_' in the direction of the larger fixed total. If L and R tie, all '_' go either way for the same distance. Hence distance = |L − R| + number of '_'.

2833.takeaway: Moves commute: the farthest distance is |L − R| plus all the wildcards, sent in the dominant direction.

p: `s = 'abcd'`, `t = 'cdab'`, `k = 2` → 2. Here `zero = 0`, `nonzero = 1` (t is s rotated by 2). M^2 gives `a = 3` (ways to end at rotation 0 from rotation 0) and `b = 2` (ways to end at a given non-zero rotation from rotation 0).

head: Quantity
Value
rows: rotations of s equal to t (r = 2)

p: The closed form agrees with a brute-force count over all sequences of k operations on six small cases (`abcd→cdab`, periodic strings such as `ababab`, `aaa`, and different k): True.

blocks.h: Why two states and a 2×2 matrix?
p: Moving a suffix of length l to the front rotates the string by l positions. After each operation the rotation offset (relative to s) changes by any l in 1…n−1. Only whether the current offset is 0 or not matters for counting, because all non-zero offsets are interchangeable. From offset 0 there are n−1 ways to a non-zero offset. From a given non-zero offset there is exactly 1 way to offset 0 and n−2 ways to other non-zero ones. This is a tiny Markov-style recurrence, so k steps are M^k.

bullets: Time: O(n²) to compare every rotation with t (string slices), plus O(log k) for the matrix power.
Space: O(n) for the doubled string.

2851.takeaway: Reduce to rotation counting: two states (offset 0 or not) with transition matrix [[0, n−1], [1, n−2]], raised to the k-th power.

p: With the peak at i, the best height at position j to its left is the minimum of maxHeights over j…i. The previous element smaller than h[i] caps everything before it, and everything after it up to i is capped by h[i]. So `left[i]` = (sum already computed for that smaller index) + h[i] × (the gap). The stack finds that index in amortised O(1), turning the naive O(n²) into O(n).

2866.takeaway: Monotonic stack for 'best sum to the left of the peak': reuse the answer at the previous smaller element and fill the gap with h[i].

p: A string of even-length blocks of equal characters is the same as a string where every aligned pair (positions 2i, 2i+1) is equal: any block of even length splits into aligned pairs of equal characters. Conversely, equal aligned pairs can be merged into valid blocks. Each unequal pair needs at least one flip and exactly one suffices, and pairs are independent.

2914.takeaway: A string is beautiful iff every aligned pair of characters is equal; count the unequal aligned pairs.

blocks.h: Why count `l` rather than the window length?
p: After shrinking, `l` points just past the last start whose subarray [start, r] still contains at least k maxima. So starts 0, 1, …, l−1 all work (a longer window to the left keeps at least as many maxima), which is exactly `l` valid subarrays ending at r. This is the 'count the complement window' trick: shrink while the condition still holds.

2962.takeaway: Sliding window that shrinks while the window still has k maxima; each right end contributes l valid starts.
